subject: math
intro: Hi, I'm Ms. Rivera. Let's plan a 6th grade lesson on measures of center using data the students collect themselves.

beats.narration: The big question is "what's typical?" — mean and median are two ways to answer it.
This standard is about recognizing that a single number can summarize a whole data set.
The "which is better" part pushes past calculating into reasoning.
beats.text: Students will be able to calculate the mean and median of a data set and explain which better represents the data when there are outliers.

beats.narration: Their own data makes them care about the answer.
beats.text: Each student writes how many minutes it took to get to school. Collect them on sticky notes on a number line on the board.

beats.narration: Adding an outlier live shows why the mean moves and the median doesn't, better than any definition.
beats.text: Find the median by ordering the sticky notes and the mean with the leveling-out idea using stacks of cubes. Then add one outlier (a 90-minute commute) and recompute both.

beats.narration: Different data sets lead to different "best" answers, which sparks good debate in the gallery walk.
beats.text: Groups get data cards (house prices, test scores, shoe sizes). They find both measures, decide which is more representative, and justify it on a mini poster.

beats.narration: The outlier is obvious on purpose; I want to see the reasoning, not a hard calculation.
beats.text: Data: 2, 3, 3, 4, 28. Find the mean and median. Which better describes a typical value? Why?

outro: Real data, a live outlier, and a justification. Your turn to plan.
